why.correct: The diagram shows fossil fuels in sedimentary layers beneath the plain.

Natural gas depends on sedimentary basins (rock).
Earth's internal heat depends on plate boundaries (rock).

The steep river and dam are in the mountains.
Right: coasts have strong, steady wind.
The diagram shows the coal under the basin, not the coast.

why.correct: The mountains have a steep river with a dam site and hot rock near a plate boundary; either fits because the resource is right there.
Faster wind carries much more energy, so the 9 m/s site would produce the most.
options: Right: highest wind speed gives the most energy.
Trees slow the wind; 3 m/s is the weakest site.
Farmland is good, but 6 m/s is slower than the offshore site.
Wind speed differs, so output differs.

why.correct: Rising air near the equator (the doldrums, where the Hadley cells begin) gives light, variable surface winds, though local sites can still be windy.

Generators work in hot climates.

why.correct: Chemical energy in the fuel becomes heat, the heat makes steam, the steam spins the turbine, and the generator turns that motion into electricity.
Steam pushes on the turbine blades and spins them. The spinning shaft drives the generator.
options: Cooling the steam is the condenser's job.
The plant makes electricity; it does not turn electricity into heat.
Right: the turbine changes the steam's energy into rotation.
Burning happens in the boiler, before the turbine.

options: Energy released as heat cannot be put back into the coal.
Right: waste heat is the largest loss.
Ash holds very little energy compared with the heat lost.
Some energy is lost in power lines, but far less than the waste heat at the plant.

why.correct: Fracking injects a high-pressure mix of water, sand and chemicals into shale rock. The cracks let trapped natural gas or oil flow to the well; the sand holds the cracks open.
options: Right: high-pressure fluid cracks the shale.
Underground coal burning is a different, rare process.
That describes surface mining of coal.

Right: wells and wastewater ponds can release volatile chemicals.
Right: each well can use millions of gallons of water.
Fracking does not produce fallout, though its wastewater can carry some natural radioactive material.
Warm water discharge comes from power plant cooling, not fracking.

why.correct: Burning gas releases about half the carbon dioxide of coal for the same electricity, so emissions fell. Methane leaks from wells offset part of the gain.
options: Fossil fuels differ in carbon dioxide per unit of energy.
Burning natural gas still releases carbon dioxide.
Right: switching from coal to gas lowers carbon dioxide per unit of energy.
Gas releases less, not more.

why.correct: Fossil fuels are energy-dense, easy to store and transport, and can be burned whenever power is needed. Their drawbacks are pollution, carbon dioxide and a fixed supply.
options: They must be mined or drilled and transported.
Right: high energy density and reliable output.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants.
They are nonrenewable.

why.correct: Separating thick bitumen from sand takes large amounts of energy (often natural gas for steam) and water, so each barrel carries extra emissions.
options: Right: extraction and upgrading use much energy.
The extra carbon dioxide comes from the energy used in processing, not gas trapped in the sand.
Bitumen is a fossil fuel, not renewable.
The bitumen is processed into crude oil, not burned at the mine.

why.correct: Cooling water from a river or cooling tower takes heat from the used steam, which condenses and is pumped back to the boiler.
options: The generator makes electricity.
The diagram shows carbon dioxide leaving through the stack; the condenser does not remove it.
Right: the condenser turns steam back into water.
Burning happens in the boiler.

why.correct: The cooling water carries only heat. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, which stresses fish and other aquatic life.
options: A coal plant's cooling water is not radioactive.
Right: the problem is heat, which lowers dissolved oxygen.
Cooling water does not touch the stack gases, so it does not carry the plant's carbon dioxide.
Cooling water does not carry coal or ash.

why.correct: The diagram shows heat leaving through the condenser's cooling water and up the stack. Turning heat into motion always discards a large share of the heat.
options: Right: the condenser and stack carry away about two thirds of the energy.
Generators are very efficient, near 98 percent.
Boilers burn coal nearly completely; the main loss is later.
Electricity leaving the generator mostly reaches the lines.

why.correct: A complete chain links burning coal to carbon dioxide, to the gas trapping heat in the atmosphere, to warming.
Surface mining strips away the overburden, destroying habitat and leaving land to be reclaimed. Acid mine drainage can pollute streams.
options: Coal mining does not use wells.
Coal releases more carbon dioxide per unit of energy than gas.
Right: large areas of habitat are destroyed.
Coal mines release dust and can cause acid mine drainage.

why.correct: The fuel is uranium (usually enriched to about 3 to 5 percent uranium-235). Water and steam only carry the heat to the turbine.
options: Water is the coolant and the source of steam; it is not split for energy.
Steam carries heat; it is not the fuel.
No fuel is burned in a nuclear reactor.
Right: uranium-235 is the fuel.

why.correct: A neutron strikes a uranium-235 nucleus, which splits into smaller nuclei, releasing a large amount of heat and 2 or 3 neutrons that can split more nuclei: a chain reaction.
options: Fission is not burning and releases no carbon dioxide.
Splitting water is a chemical change, not a nuclear one.
Right: splitting heavy nuclei is fission.
Joining light nuclei is fusion, which powers the sun, not today's reactors.

why.correct: Control rods are made of materials that absorb neutrons. Lowering them in takes neutrons out of the chain reaction; pulling them out lets it speed up.
options: Spent fuel is stored in pools and casks, not in control rods.
Right: absorbing neutrons controls the rate.
Fuel rods hold the uranium; control rods do not add fuel.
Water carries the heat.

options: Right: half the atoms decay in one half-life.
Decay never quite reaches zero; each half-life halves what is left.
How long a sample is dangerous depends on many half-lives and the type of radiation.
Half-life counts atoms that decay; the decay products still have mass.

Long-lived isotopes remain after the short-lived ones decay.
After one half-life, half of that isotope is still there.

why.correct: Fission in the fuel rods releases the heat; water carries it to the steam generator.
options: Right: fission in the fuel rods.
Nothing is burned in a nuclear reactor.
The cooling tower removes heat; it does not supply it.
The generator makes electricity from motion.

why.correct: More neutrons are absorbed, the chain reaction slows or stops, less heat is made and the turbine slows.
options: Lowering the rods slows fission; it does not speed it up.
Uranium does not turn into coal.
With less heat, less steam reaches the turbine.
Right: absorbing neutrons slows the reaction.

why.correct: Radioactive fission products keep giving off heat after the reaction stops. Without cooling water, the fuel overheats and can melt, as at Fukushima in 2011.
options: Heat flows from the core to the turbine, not back.
A dry cooling tower removes less heat; it does not add any.
Right: decay heat continues after shutdown.
Control rods absorb neutrons; they do not make heat.

why.correct: Advantage: no carbon dioxide or smoke while running, because nothing is burned. Disadvantage: radioactive spent fuel that must be stored for thousands of years, or the risk of an accident.

options: Right: Chernobyl was the worst nuclear accident.
A tanker grounding is a petroleum accident.
A mine collapse is a coal mining accident.
A dam failure is a hazard of dams, not of nuclear plants.

why.correct: Natural uranium is about 0.7 percent uranium-235. Most reactors need fuel with about 3 to 5 percent to keep the chain reaction going.
options: Natural uranium is weakly radioactive; enrichment raises its uranium-235 share.
Uranium is mined from a fixed supply; enrichment does not change that.
Uranium is not burned and contains no carbon.
Right: the fissile isotope must be concentrated.

why.correct: Biomass is recently living organic matter: wood, charcoal, crop waste, dung, and fuels made from crops.
options: Natural gas is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years.
Uranium is a mined mineral.
Sunlight is solar energy, not biomass.
Right: dung is organic matter from living things.

why.correct: Yeast ferments the sugars in corn, sugarcane or other crops into ethanol, which is distilled and blended into gasoline.
options: That process makes biodiesel.
Splitting water makes hydrogen.
Right: fermentation of crop sugars.
Refining crude oil makes gasoline, not ethanol.

why.correct: Biodiesel is made by reacting vegetable oils (soybean, canola, palm) or animal fats so they can run diesel engines.
options: Cooled natural gas is liquefied natural gas, a fossil fuel.
Right: plant oils or animal fats.
Fermented and distilled sugar is ethanol.
Liquid coal is a fossil fuel product.

why.correct: Indoor smoke from wood, charcoal, crop waste or dung harms the lungs and is a major cause of illness and early death in poorer countries, especially for women and children.
options: Right: indoor smoke is a leading health risk.
Wood is not a meaningful radiation source.
A home cooking fire does not heat streams.

Burning wood releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat.

options: Most gasoline in the United States already contains about 10 percent ethanol.
Corn is regrown each year, so ethanol is renewable.
Right: land, water and fertilizer use and competition with food.
Ethanol makes no radioactive waste.

why.correct: Anaerobic decomposition of manure, food waste or sewage makes biogas, which is mostly methane, a renewable form of the main gas in natural gas.

Right: anaerobic digestion makes methane-rich biogas.
Ethanol comes from fermenting crop sugars, not manure digestion.
Coal forms over millions of years.

Corn gives 75 GJ per hectare.
Soybeans give 20 GJ per hectare.

why.correct: The diagram shows growing plants storing carbon from the air through photosynthesis.

Burning biomass releases carbon dioxide, soot and other pollutants.

Storing heat in a thick floor is passive solar design.
Burning fuel is not solar energy.

An electric heater uses electricity made elsewhere, not the building's design.

Right: the sun's angle changes with the seasons.
Blocking winter sun would defeat the design.
An overhang shades; it does not cool by collecting rain.

options: Right: variable output needs storage or backup.
Panels usually last about 25 to 30 years.
Sunlight striking a panel releases nothing.
Each panel collects the light that falls on it; it does not use up sunlight elsewhere.

These plants heat a fluid; they do not make hydrogen.
Storing heat in rock is passive heating, not electricity generation.

Panels do not block the wind enough to cool a desert.

Panels release nothing while making electricity.

Output is zero at night.
Panels contain silicon, metals and glass that must be mined and made.
